summary: Vision paper with preliminary results. Credo takes an LLM harness found by Meta-Harness search and has claude-opus-4-7 recover a typed declarative description: a DAG 'skeleton' of named steps, typed 'beliefs' (runtime signals), 'policies' that pick a physical implementation (model, k, strategy) from beliefs, and prompt templates. Each primitive is tagged functional or source-specific and catalogued with provenance; a compiler binds catalogued primitives into a new harness.py for an unseen target. On four QA/reasoning workloads (finance, legal, math, polyreason) with gemma3-12b/gemma4-31b workers and a gpt-5-mini judge, recover-then-compile reproduces the source harness within ±0.011 accuracy and ±0.013 ¢/q on 100 questions. Cross-domain compilation helps two retrieval transfers (15.7 to 28.3; 43.4 to 66.3), modestly helps math, and hurts polyreason relative to brief-only (38.7/34.9 vs 43.3).

claims.claim: A recovered declarative description preserves the behaviour of the searched harness: round-trip accuracy within ±0.011 and per-question cost within ±0.013 ¢/q across four domains
claims.evidence: Table 2: 3 source harnesses per domain x 3 compile replicates on a 100-question in-distribution split. Matching cost as well as accuracy is a sensible guard against the compiler solving the task its own way. But with n=100 the per-run accuracy standard error is about 0.045-0.05, no per-question agreement or trace comparison is reported, and aggregate matches cannot show that the same method was reconstructed.

claims.claim: Every recovered skeleton step is functional (0 source-specific steps), so logical plans transfer cleanly
claims.evidence: Table 3 counts come from the LLM level-tagger's own labels; no human or behavioural validation of the tags. Transfer results show plans do not always transfer usefully (math to polyreason lands below brief-only).

claims.claim: Catalogued primitives compile into working harnesses for unseen targets without re-searching
claims.evidence: Fig. 3, cross-distribution splits (300 queries), same models and judge. legal to finance 15.7 to 28.3 (searched 27.7); finance to legal 43.4 to 66.3 (searched 73.4); polyreason to math 39.6 to 44.6/45.4; math to polyreason 38.7/34.9 vs brief-only 43.3, a regression. Two of four transfers clearly help. Replicate counts and intervals for Fig. 3 are not given.

claims.claim: Searched harnesses overfit to the source domain while Credo-compiled harnesses do not
claims.evidence: Searched polyreason falls 72 to 47 and math 67 to 37 from in-distribution to cross-distribution. Compiled harnesses are reported only on the target cross-distribution split, so 'do not exhibit these drops' compares different quantities. The searched harness was selected on the in-distribution split, which predicts some drop.

claims.claim: The approach achieves more than an order of magnitude in cost savings over agentic harness search
claims.evidence: One recover-and-compile call costs $2.3-2.8 against $43-72 for a 10-iteration Meta-Harness search (Table 2). But the catalog only exists because the source domains were searched first, so savings apply to later targets and are not net. In 2 of 4 transfers the compiled harness is below the searched one or below brief-only.

patterns.note: Compares search-from-scratch (Meta-Harness) with compile-from-catalog on the same workers, judge and splits. The catalog is far cheaper per new target and matches search on legal to finance. It recovers 76% of the gap on finance to legal and hurts on math to polyreason. Searched harnesses lose 25-30 points off-distribution, a caution for any searched or self-improving harness.

Proposes representing a harness as a declarative static workflow: a DAG skeleton of named steps, typed beliefs computed at declared plan points, and belief-conditioned policies selecting implementations, compiled to a fixed harness.py. No comparison of declarative-compiled against imperative or agent-loop harnesses on the same budget; the round trip only shows the representation loses little.

An LLM (the abstractor) emits the step DAG, but it does so offline, from existing code, to build a reusable description. It is not a runtime task planner and there is no parallel scheduling; DAG accuracy is not evaluated and no planner-DAG baseline is run.

Searched harnesses include small-to-large cascades and the compiler reliably picks routing primitives for retrieval targets; routing is never isolated. Transferred policies carry the source's cost operating point, which hurt math to polyreason.
Typed, named beliefs and per-primitive provenance make branch conditions loggable and comparable across runs; belief-selectivity drift is proposed as a staleness signal. Not evaluated.
All accuracy is graded by a gpt-5-mini judge with per-dataset rules; no agreement check against gold labels or humans is reported, even where exact-match answers exist.

methodology.sample: Four constructed workloads (finance and legal retrieval over document pools; math and polyreason reasoning), each with 100 search, 100 in-distribution and 300 cross-distribution questions; 3 searched source harnesses per domain; four source-to-target transfers.
methodology.baselines: Original searched harness (round trip); brief-only compile, single-domain catalog, open-library catalog and the target's own searched harness (transfer).
methodology.models: gemma3-12b / gemma4-31b workers (vLLM); claude-opus-4-7 for search proposer, abstractor and compiler; gpt-5-mini judge.
methodology.variance: Round trip: 3 seeds x 3 compile replicates, means only. Transfer: 'within run-to-run variation' asserted, intervals not shown.
methodology.ablations: Catalog access (none, single-domain, open-library). No ablation of primitive types (skeleton vs beliefs vs policies vs templates).
methodology.contamination_controls: Sandbox prevents evaluation leakage during search; public benchmarks may be known to models.
methodology.languages: Python harness programs; tasks are QA and reasoning, not code generation

standards.artifacts: None for Credo. Only Meta-Harness (third-party searcher) is linked.

biases.detail: 100-question fidelity split, 3 source harnesses per domain, 4 transfers.
Accuracy everywhere comes from one LLM judge without validation.
Behavioural fidelity is inferred from aggregate accuracy and cost, not per-question agreement or trace equivalence.
Authors evaluate their own system against a harness search they configured; compiler and abstractor use the same frontier model as the searcher.
No code, prompts, catalogs or compiled harnesses released.
'More than an order of magnitude in cost savings' ignores that the catalog requires prior searches and that half the transfers trail the searched or brief-only harness.

coi.detail: Academic authors; builds on their own earlier Credo system.

verdict_reason: A clear idea with sensible checks (cost as well as accuracy in the round trip, explicit brief-only and searched references in transfer), but it is a preliminary vision paper. The samples are small, the judge is unvalidated, nothing is released, and transfer helps only 2 of 4 times. The cost-saving headline omits the searches the catalog depends on, and the paper concerns QA/reasoning harnesses, not coding agents.
applicability: Indirect. For the team's DAG question, Credo argues that whatever workflow structure exists (step DAG, branch signals, model-choice rules, prompt templates) should be kept as a typed, declarative, provenance-tagged artifact that can be reviewed and reused, not buried in one host's code. That fits keeping workflow definitions in committed, host-neutral files that qr can verify. The evidence suggests reuse works between like tasks (retrieval to retrieval) and can hurt when the source's cost/accuracy policies do not fit the target, so primitives shared across the four repos would need per-repo evaluation rather than blind import. Searched or tuned workflows lost 25-30 points off-distribution, a warning against tuning a workflow DAG on one repo's tasks and rolling it out to the others. It does not show that a declarative DAG beats a plain agent loop, and no coding tasks were tested.

conflicts_with.detail: MESH-Harness reports that searched modular harnesses beat Meta-Harness on held-out test splits at lower search and test cost. Credo finds Meta-Harness-searched harnesses fall 25-30 points on cross-distribution splits. MESH's test sets are disjoint from validation but drawn from the same task distribution, so the two results are compatible only if searched-harness gains are distribution-bound. MESH's cross-model transfer test does not cover cross-distribution shift.
